title: Eid al-Fitr: joy
tomorrow: Eid's over. does the fasting just stop?

lines: HOW MUCH JOY FITS A HOLY DAY?
IT CAME UP IN HIS HOUSE.
cards: The night the moon is spotted, phones start buzzing: Eid Mubarak, Eid Mubarak. By morning there are new clothes, a crowded prayer, and trays of sweets going door to door.
And in some families, the same yearly argument: how much celebrating fits a holy day? Music or no music? The question is old.
It came up in the Prophet's own house.

teach.h: ABU BAKR: NOT IN THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: 'A'isha remembers an Eid, in Sahih al-Bukhari. Two girls are singing in her room. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is lying down, his face turned away.
Then Abu Bakr walks in, her father, and he's upset: musical instruments of Satan, in the house of the Messenger of God? Hear his side fairly.
This is a house where revelation comes down. He's guarding it, and he loves the man whose house it is. And the Prophet's answer: Abu Bakr, every people has its Eid, and this is our Eid.

On another Eid, 'A'isha says, men from Abyssinia played with shields and spears, and she watched from behind him until she'd had enough. So on Eid, joy wasn't a break from religion. It was part of the day.
Muslims still read that scene in more than one way.
Some take it as room for song and celebration on festival days. Others note it was girls singing, on a festival, and draw the lines on music more tightly.

Both start from the same room. And the joy has a door. Before the Eid prayer, the Prophet made zakat al-fitr a duty, a gift of food paid before people go out to pray, so the poor have something to eat on Eid too.

how: On Eid al-Fitr Muslims pay zakat al-fitr before the morning prayer, gather for the Eid prayer, then visit family and friends with food, new clothes and gifts for children.

o: the festival that ends Ramadan, with prayer and joy
a voluntary fast kept the day after Ramadan ends
the final night of Ramadan, spent awake in prayer

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: guarded the house from the singing

s: Abu Bakr objected to singing in the Prophet's house on Eid
and the Prophet answered: every people has its Eid, and this is our Eid.
once the fast is broken, Eid has no religious part left
Eid has its own prayer, and zakat al-fitr is paid before it.
Muslims all read the Eid singing scene the same way
some see room for song on festivals; others draw the lines on music more tightly.

games.q: at the Eid lunch your uncle wants it quiet, no music; your cousins want the speaker on. everyone looks at you. what does the old scene give you?
o: the cousins win: the report shows anything goes on Eid.
the uncle wins: Abu Bakr was right to stop the singing.
Eid has room for joy; on music, Muslims differ, so make room for both.
games.why: the Prophet let the singing go on: this is our Eid. but Abu Bakr's care for a holy house is real, and readers still differ on music. joy wins; the volume is for the family to work out.

practice: Bring to mind someone who might spend the next holiday, any holiday, a little on their own. Write them a short message now, warm and specific, the kind that would make them smile. Send it, or keep it ready for the day.

wordCard.voice: Eid al-Fitr: the festival of breaking the fast, the day after Ramadan. A prayer, food for the poor, and joy.

orig.note: Arabic: the festival of breaking the fast, which ends Ramadan.

carryVoice: For the road: joy is worship, defended once in the Prophet's own house. Let the tables be full.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 949–950, 952, 987 ('A'isha: two girls singing on Eid; Abu Bakr objects; 'every people has its Eid, and this is our Eid'; the Abyssinians with shields and spears)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1503 (Ibn 'Umar: zakat al-fitr made a duty, to be paid before people go out to the prayer)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1609 (zakat al-fitr as food for the poor)
